rv.q: As an extrapolation of the author’s themes, this is solid and acutely relevant.

But the production is hampered by its own cleverness, the elliptic storytelling a distraction from the clarity and intrigue of this story’s psychological questions around fear, sexual desire and moral corruption.
A masterclass in how a Gothic novel adaptation should be done whilst adding an extra twist or two along the way.

The doubling of Miles and Flora with the silent adult roles of Quint and Jessel was borne of necessity (as Lloyd Malcolm’s programme note explains) but it succeeds in complicating the disturbing relationships between the children and the deceased adults even further.
So regardless of whether one has read the original text, this production can be seen on its own terms, and it is exciting and convincing.
With every retelling, the story changes slightly – but the sense of Gothic chill remains.
But there’s a quid pro quo to pay for the subversion of the genre’s norms, one I felt to be a little too much for what came back in return.
This is a strong production with powerful performances that breathe new life into a classic tale.
This is on it own terms an entirely original, exciting and thoroughly convincing take on the original.
The Turn of the Screw is effective in delivering a sense of the paranormal activities and enough doubt that the Governess may be mistaken to drive the show.
It’s a dark, seasonal treat to experience front on and full throttle!

The creative team's reimagining of the relationships between the Governess and the characters is exceptional and works upon ideas already implicit in James' original story by pushing them to their limits.
This is a cleverly done production with a fantastic cast, leaving us questioning the series of events and inspiring me to reread the novella.
I was won over almost immediately, largely down to Amy Tara’s performance as the Governess.
The Turn of the Screw is a solid production with a strong cast and deserves its place as a ghost story on stage.

The original is said to be the inspiration for The Women in Black, but Emilia playwright Morgan Lloyd Malcolm’s stage adaptation of Henry James’ novella The Turn of the Screw is missing the scares and the psychology which would support such a claim.
The uncertainty of the story comes to the fore and the real ghosts reveal themselves to be the ones in our own minds.
If you have never experienced a horror theatre show, this is definitely an experiential piece with lots of strength.
Allpress’s direction was ambitious and inventive.
Overall, The Turn of the Screw is a creative but respectful reimagining of James’ novella, enlivened by an eerie soundscape and flashes of visual ingenuity.

cn.t: Malcolm's adaptation of the gothic classic earns praise for atmospheric staging and psychological depth, though critics split on its modern framing device and uneven pacing. Strong performances and bold feminist angle impress most.
